The Broncos were penalized 8 times for 56 yards and the Colts 4 times for 30 yards. Here's a breakdown of those penalties.

The Broncos had 4 penalties for 26 yards that were clear-cut and will get called every time. (offsides, facemask on ball carrier, eye gouge, and unsportsmanlike contuct)

The Colts had 3 penalties for 25 yards that were clear-cut. (false start, interference with opportunity to catch on a punt, illegal touched pass)

The Broncos had 3 penalties for 25 yards which can be considered more subjective, but still ones that will easily get called. (unnecessary roughness (Ward hit on Hilton), illegal use of hands, defensive holding (not the FG attempt))

The Colts had 1 penalty for 5 yards which can be considered more subjective, but still ones that will easily get called. (defensive pass interference in the end zone)

The Broncos had 1 penalty for 5 yards that was complete shit, the defensive holding on the FG attempt.

You can say that the Broncos were called for twice as many penalties (8 vs 4), but 3 of those penalties happened on the final Colts drive. You can say the defensive holding was crap because it was, but the other 2 penalties are ones that will get thrown every time when the refs see them.

I can't speak to the other officiating crews the Broncos have had this season, but outside of that defensive holding call on the FG attempt, I don't see any evidence that the refs were biased against the Broncos in that game.

He appealed the suspension and got it overturned (but was still fined). Given Ward's history of being a repeat offender, I suspect that a suspension was the next logical progression, but he'll appeal and it will likely get overturned because the helmet to helmet contact was incidental.

As far as Adam Jones, I believe that was his first incident of getting fined for an on the field action and it happened in the pre-season, two factors which make it significantly less likely that he would get suspended for that.

I don't know enough about economics to be able to evaluate everything this guy is saying. But we should recognize a few things about his article and the guy himself. He is using misleading statistics. The claim makes it sound like this change would create instant millionaires out of everybody, but he uses average savings by the US government, per house hold, on things like interest which takes time to accrue. This is misleading for three reasons. One it is not instant, this is definitely over a long period of time. Two, "average house hold," does not really hold much meaning in this context because it would be a heavily skewed statistic, a "median house hold," would be a better statistic to be used. Three the government is making these savings, not the citizens (although if his theory is correct than it might have a net benefit for taxpayers.) A few more things, this story is from a high school teachers blog. This doesn't mean he is wrong, or his analysis is wrong. But it is something people should recognize and consider when evaluating this guys work. Also his focus in the article is on fiat money, not that this is wrong. Just that when discussing economics usually we are more concerned with wealth, which is different. Again not that what he is saying is wrong (although I would have a few questions for him about how he thinks the government will be more efficient than the semi-competitive US financial market), just that these are a few things we should consider.
